question: What is the primary goal of community mobilisation?

options.A: Enforcing strict national health laws in rural villages
options.B: Replacing traditional healers with modern medical doctors
options.C: Collecting financial taxes for local health clinics
options.D: Empowering community members to solve local problems together

explanation: Community mobilisation focuses on bringing people together so they can take charge of their own health issues and find local solutions. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h1)

question: Why do health programs built on community mobilisation usually last longer than top-down programs?

options.A: Because government nurses supervise every single household daily
options.B: Because the community takes ownership and actively participates in the solutions
options.C: Because traditional beliefs are completely ignored by the project
options.D: Because foreign donors provide unlimited financial support forever

explanation: When people are part of creating the solution, they care for it and maintain it long after external workers leave. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h1)

question: Which principle ensures that vulnerable and quiet voices are heard during community health projects?
explanation: Equity makes sure that everyone, especially the poor and marginalized, gets a fair chance to participate and benefit. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h2)

question: A nurse wants to start a health program in a village. When should community participation ideally begin?

options.A: When the government evaluates the final report
options.B: After the foreign funding runs out completely
options.C: From the very beginning during problem identification
options.D: Only when the clinic building is finished

explanation: True participation starts at the planning stage so the community actually helps identify what needs fixing. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h2)

question: What is a major benefit of working with a mobilized community for a nurse?

options.A: Health messages spread easily through local networks
options.B: All diseases are completely eradicated overnight
options.C: Nurses no longer need to write patient records
options.D: The government stops paying salaries to health workers

explanation: When a community is mobilized, people talk to each other about health, making health education spread fast. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h3)

question: How does community mobilisation directly support primary health care goals?

options.A: By building large tertiary teaching hospitals in every small town
options.B: By stopping patients from visiting traditional birth attendants
options.C: By helping people manage preventable diseases and improve local sanitation
options.D: By replacing community health workers with paid international staff

explanation: Primary health care focuses on prevention and community-level action, which mobilisation directly achieves. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h3)

question: Why is it important to involve traditional and religious leaders in health mobilisation?

options.A: They hold strong moral authority and influence public opinion
options.B: They write the national nursing curriculum
options.C: They are the only people who understand modern medicine
options.D: They are required by law to fund all local pharmacies

explanation: Traditional and religious leaders are respected, and their approval helps community members trust health initiatives. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h4)

question: A nurse wants to improve maternal health in a rural area where many women use traditional birth attendants. What is the best approach regarding these attendants?

options.A: Ignore them completely and tell pregnant women never to speak to them
options.B: Ask them to close their businesses and work as hospital cleaners
options.C: Arrest them immediately for practicing medicine without a formal license
options.D: Engage and train them to recognize danger signs and refer women to the clinic

explanation: Working with traditional birth attendants builds a safe bridge instead of creating conflict, saving more mothers. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h4)

question: What is the very first step a nurse should take when starting community mobilisation?

options.A: Entry and sensitization with local leaders
options.B: Building a brand new brick health clinic
options.C: Punishing people who miss immunization days
options.D: Writing the final project evaluation report

explanation: You must enter respectfully and introduce yourself to leaders before trying to assess needs or plan actions. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h5)

question: During which step of mobilisation do community members and nurses figure out what resources and tasks are needed?
explanation: Action planning is where the community maps out tasks, responsibilities, and timelines using local resources. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h5)

question: Which tool involves community members drawing maps and calendars to show their own health and resource realities?
explanation: PRA tools allow people to visually map their village resources and health risks themselves. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h6)

question: Why are local drama and folk media effective strategies in community mobilisation?

options.A: They provide a strict legal punishment for people who ignore health advice
options.B: They communicate health messages using culturally familiar and engaging entertainment
options.C: They force the government to release emergency healthcare funds instantly
options.D: They replace the need for any professional medical staff in the clinic

explanation: Drama and songs capture attention and break down complex health ideas into relatable stories. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h6)

question: What is 'elite capture' in the context of community mobilisation?

options.A: When foreign donors pull out all financial support suddenly
options.B: When only wealthy or powerful individuals benefit from or control the project
options.C: When the local police arrest community health workers unjustly
options.D: When traditional healers refuse to speak with modern nurses

explanation: Elite capture happens when powerful community members take over resources meant for everyone. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h7)

question: How should a nurse handle community apathy caused by previous failed health projects?

options.A: Threaten to withhold all future medical treatments from families
options.B: Be honest, transparent, and follow through on small achievable goals to rebuild trust
options.C: Abandon the village and find a wealthier community to work with
options.D: Scold the community for not appreciating government assistance

explanation: Trust is rebuilt slowly through honesty and delivering small, visible successes together. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h7)

question: Which factor is most critical for ensuring the long-term sustainability of a community health project?

options.A: Total community ownership and local leadership
options.B: Permanent supervision by foreign medical doctors
options.C: Keeping all project funds hidden in a secret bank account
options.D: Banning local meetings after the project is completed

explanation: When a community feels the project belongs to them, they maintain it long after external support ends. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h8)

question: Which of the following is an example of participatory monitoring?

options.A: The health minister deciding project success without visiting the village
options.B: Community members tracking how many latrines they have built together
options.C: An external auditor writing a secret report in the capital city
options.D: A nurse counting clinic pills behind closed doors at night

explanation: Participatory monitoring involves the local people themselves measuring their own progress and output. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h8)
